what_its_for: Methoxsalen is used to treat certain skin conditions, including psoriasis (scaly, itchy patches on skin), vitiligo (loss of skin color in patches), and certain types of skin lymphoma (a type of skin cancer). It works by making your skin more sensitive to ultraviolet (UV) light, which is then used during a special light therapy treatment called PUVA (Psoralen plus Ultraviolet A light).
how_to_take: Methoxsalen comes as a capsule or liquid that you swallow. Always take it with food or milk to help prevent an upset stomach. You must take your dose exactly 1.5 to 2 hours before your scheduled UVA light therapy session — not before or after this window. Do not take extra doses on your own. If you are using the Uvadex liquid form, it is given by a healthcare professional during a special procedure called photopheresis, where your blood is treated with the medication and UV light outside your body.
dosing: Your doctor will decide your dose based on your body weight and the condition being treated. A common starting dose is 0.4 mg per kilogram of body weight, taken about 2 hours before light therapy. You should not take methoxsalen more than once every 48 hours (every other day at most). Your doctor will slowly adjust your dose and the amount of UV light based on how your skin responds. Never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose or miss your light therapy session, do not double your next dose. Contact your doctor or clinic to reschedule your session. It is very important that the medication and the light therapy are coordinated — taking the pill without the light therapy (or vice versa) will not work correctly and can cause problems.
storage: Store methoxsalen capsules at room temperature, away from heat, light, and moisture. Keep it in a cool, dry place (around 59–77°F or 15–25°C). Keep it out of the bathroom. Keep all medicines safely out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medication after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: For at least 24 hours after taking methoxsalen AND after your light therapy session, you must: (1) Protect your skin from sunlight — stay indoors or cover all exposed skin with protective clothing and use sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher. (2) Wear special UV-blocking sunglasses outdoors AND indoors near bright windows to protect your eyes from UV damage — failure to do so can cause serious eye damage, including cataracts. (3) Avoid tanning beds, sunlamps, or any other UV light sources. Avoid eating limes, figs, parsley, parsnips, mustard, carrots, and celery in large amounts, as these foods may increase your skin's sensitivity to light. Avoid alcohol if your doctor advises it.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: severe sunburn, blistering, or painful redness of the skin; eye pain or vision changes; nausea, vomiting, or severe stomach pain; signs of an allergic reaction (rash, swelling of face or throat, trouble breathing); unusual moles, new skin growths, or skin color changes; dizziness or feeling faint; or signs of skin infection (warmth, swelling, pus, or increasing redness). Also tell your doctor if your condition is not improving after several weeks of treatment.
when_it_works: Methoxsalen does not work overnight. Most patients begin to notice improvement in their skin condition after several weeks to months of regular PUVA therapy sessions. For psoriasis, many patients see significant clearing after 20 to 30 sessions. For vitiligo, it may take 6 to 12 months or longer to see repigmentation (return of skin color). Be patient and continue treatment as directed by your doctor.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Methoxsalen may harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Use effective birth control during treatment. Children: This medicine is generally not recommended for children under 12 years of age. Elderly: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects; your doctor will monitor you carefully. Kidney or Liver Problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as methoxsalen is processed by the liver and may need dose adjustments. Skin Cancer History: If you have a history of skin cancer or many moles, tell your doctor before starting this medication, as UV light therapy may increase your risk. People with lupus, porphyria, or other light-sensitive conditions should not use this medicine.
